<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-kernel-methods">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">[{{< fa star >}}]{.advanced title="MAS8607 Content"} Understand <span class="xref-no-num">[kernel methods @sec-kernel-methods]</span>, including the idea of the kernel trick and feature inner products.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-kernel-methods" hidden>

### Core Idea

<span class="xref-no-num">[Kernel methods @sec-kernel-methods]</span> allow us to use very rich (even infinite-dimensional) feature spaces without explicitly computing the features.

The key observation is that, for a <span class="xref-no-num">[linear model @def-linear-model]</span> trained using squared error loss, predictions can be written in terms of **inner products in feature space**.

---

### Key Observation

Let $\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})$ be the feature map and $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ the design matrix.

The prediction at a new point $\mathbf{x}_\star$ can be written as

$$
f_{\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}(\mathbf{x}_\star)
=
\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_\star)^\top \boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top
(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top)^{-1}
\mathbf{y}.
$$

Crucially, the feature map only appears through inner products of the form

$$
\langle \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i), \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_j) \rangle.
$$

---

### Kernel Trick

Define a **kernel function**

$$
k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')
=
\langle \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}), \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}') \rangle.
$$

Then all computations can be expressed in terms of $k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')$, without explicitly computing $\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})$.

This is called the **kernel trick**.

---

### Why This Matters

This allows us to:

- work with very high-dimensional feature spaces;
- even use **infinite-dimensional features**;
- avoid explicitly computing $\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})$.

For example, we can define models of the form

$$
f(\mathbf{x})
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\alpha_i \, k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}_i),
$$

where the model depends only on the training data and the kernel function.

---

### Interpretation

- Kernel methods implicitly define a feature space.
- Instead of computing features directly, we compute inner products via $k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')$.
- This enables highly flexible models while keeping computations tractable.

---

### Key Points

- Kernel methods rely on inner products in <span class="xref-no-num">[feature space @def-feature-space]</span>.
- A kernel function satisfies
  $$
  k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = \langle \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}), \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}') \rangle.
  $$
- The **kernel trick** avoids explicit computation of features.
- This allows use of high-dimensional or infinite-dimensional feature spaces.
- Predictions can be written in terms of kernels and training data only.
- **This content is examinable for MAS8607 only.**

</div>
</div>


<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-kernel-definition">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">[{{< fa star >}}]{.advanced title="MAS8607 Content"} Be able to state the definition of a <span class="xref-no-num">[kernel @def-kernel]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-kernel-definition" hidden>

### Definition

A function

$$
k : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}
$$

is called a **kernel** if it satisfies:

1. **Symmetry**
   $$
   k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) = k(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x})
   \quad \text{for all } \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{X}.
   $$

2. **Positive semi-definiteness**
   For all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, all $\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_n \in \mathcal{X}$, and all $w_1,\dots,w_n \in \mathbb{R}$,

   $$
   \sum_{r=1}^n \sum_{s=1}^n
   w_r w_s \, k(\mathbf{x}_r,\mathbf{x}_s)
   \geq 0.
   $$

---

### Equivalent Matrix Interpretation

Given points $\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_n$, define the matrix

$$
\mathbf{K}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
k(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_1) & \cdots & k(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_n) \\
\vdots & & \vdots \\
k(\mathbf{x}_n,\mathbf{x}_1) & \cdots & k(\mathbf{x}_n,\mathbf{x}_n)
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Then $k$ is a kernel if and only if, for any choice of $\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_n$, the matrix $\mathbf{K}$ satisfies: 

- $\mathbf{K}$ is **symmetric**, and  
- $\mathbf{K}$ is **positive semi-definite**, i.e.
  $$
  \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{K} \mathbf{w} \geq 0
  \quad \text{for all } \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^n.
  $$

---

### Interpretation

A kernel can be thought of as an **inner product in feature space**:

$$
k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')
=
\langle \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}), \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}') \rangle,
$$

for some (possibly high-dimensional) feature map $\boldsymbol{\phi}$.

---

### Key Points

- A kernel is a symmetric, positive semi-definite function.
- It defines a positive semi-definite matrix for any dataset.
- Kernels correspond to inner products in a feature space.
- **This content is examinable for MAS8607 only.**

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-kernel-methods-limitations">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">[{{< fa star >}}]{.advanced title="MAS8607 Content"} Understand the strengths and limitations of <span class="xref-no-num">[kernel methods @sec-kernel-methods]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-kernel-methods-limitations" hidden>

### Why Kernel Methods Work

<span class="xref-no-num">[Kernel methods @sec-kernel-methods]</span> are effective for tasks such as regression and classification because they allow us to work in **high-dimensional feature spaces**.

In these feature spaces, the structure of the data (e.g. separation between classes) can become easier to identify.

---

### Key Limitation

Unlike other <span class="xref-no-num">[featurisation @sec-featurisation]</span> methods:

- <span class="xref-no-num">[variable selection @sec-variable-selection]</span>, and  
- <span class="xref-no-num">[dimensionality reduction @sec-dim-reduction]</span>,

the feature space in kernel methods is **not learned from the data**.

Instead:

- the feature space is **completely determined by the choice of kernel**.

---

### Consequence

This means:

- performance depends heavily on choosing an appropriate kernel;
- selecting a good kernel often requires **expert knowledge** of the problem.

---

### Kernel Learning

One approach is to use a **parametric family of kernels**

$$
\{k_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}\}_{\boldsymbol{\psi} \in \Psi}
$$

and learn the parameters $\boldsymbol{\psi}$ from the data.

However:

- designing a suitable family $\{k_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}\}$ can still be difficult.

---

### Motivation for Neural Networks

Because of these limitations, **neural networks** are often preferred in modern machine learning:

- they **learn features automatically from data**;
- they do not require manually specifying a feature map or kernel.

---

### Key Points

- Kernel methods work by mapping data into high-dimensional feature spaces.
- The feature space is fixed by the choice of kernel.
- Choosing a good kernel is difficult and problem-dependent.
- Kernel learning attempts to tune kernels using data.
- Neural networks provide a fully data-driven alternative.
- **This content is examinable for MAS8607 only.**

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-neural-networks">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand the basic idea of <span class="xref-no-num">[neural networks @sec-nn]</span> and the role of <span class="xref-no-num">[activation functions @sec-activation]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-neural-networks" hidden>

### What is a Neural Network?

A **neural network** is a parametric model

$$
f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} : \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}
$$

that represents a function as a **composition of layers**.

Each layer applies:

1. a linear transformation;
2. a nonlinear **activation function**.

This allows neural networks to represent highly complex, nonlinear relationships between input and output.

---

### Role of Activation Functions

An **activation function** is a function

$$
\sigma : \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}
$$

applied after a linear transformation.

**Key idea:**

- Without activation functions, a neural network reduces to a **linear model**.
- Nonlinearity is what gives neural networks their expressive power.

---

### Common Activation Functions

#### Logistic (Sigmoid)

$$
\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}
$$

- Output in $(0,1)$
- Useful for binary classification
- Can suffer from **vanishing gradients**

---

#### ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit)

$$
\sigma(z) = \max(0, z)
$$

- Most widely used in practice
- Simple and computationally efficient
- Avoids vanishing gradient for $z > 0$

---

#### Leaky ReLU

$$
\sigma(z) =
\begin{cases}
z & z > 0 \\
\alpha z & z \leq 0
\end{cases}
$$

- Fixes the **dying ReLU problem**
- Keeps a small gradient when $z < 0$

---

### Key Properties

- Activation functions introduce **nonlinearity**
- Neural networks are **compositions of linear maps + nonlinearities**
- Output is typically a **continuous function** of the input
- Choice of activation function affects training performance

---

### Key Points

- Neural networks are flexible nonlinear models.
- They are built from layers of linear transformations and activation functions.
- Nonlinearity is essential — otherwise the model is linear.
- Common activations: sigmoid, ReLU, leaky ReLU.
- Activation choice affects optimisation and performance.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-nn-regularisation-intuition">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand why <span class="xref-no-num">[regularisation @sec-regularisation]</span> is important in neural networks.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-nn-regularisation-intuition" hidden>

### Why Regularisation is Needed

Neural networks often have **very large numbers of parameters**, sometimes far exceeding the number of training data points.

This makes them highly flexible and capable of fitting training data extremely well.

However, this also creates a risk of <span class="xref-no-num">[over-fitting @sec-perf-assess]</span>, where the model performs well on training data but poorly on new data.

---

### Key Idea

**Regularisation** refers to techniques that improve the model’s ability to generalise to new data.

It works by:

- reducing overfitting;
- encouraging simpler or more stable solutions;
- preventing the model from fitting noise in the data.

---

### Neural Network Setting

In neural networks:

- models are often **over-parameterised**;
- optimisation is **high-dimensional and complex**;
- yet good generalisation is often observed in practice.

This makes regularisation especially important, even if it is not always fully understood theoretically.

---

### Two Types

There are two main types of regularisation:

1. <span class="xref-no-num">[explicit regularisation @sec-explicit-reg-nn]</span>  
   → directly modifies the training objective or model

2. <span class="xref-no-num">[implicit regularisation @sec-implicit-reg-nn]</span>  
   → arises from the training process itself

---

### Key Points

- Neural networks are highly flexible and prone to overfitting.
- Regularisation improves generalisation performance.
- It is especially important in large, over-parameterised models.
- There are both explicit and implicit forms of regularisation.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-nn-regularisation-types">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand <span class="xref-no-num">[explicit @sec-explicit-reg-nn]</span> and <span class="xref-no-num">[implicit regularisation @sec-implicit-reg-nn]</span> in neural networks.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-nn-regularisation-types" hidden>

### Explicit Regularisation

<span class="xref-no-num">[Explicit regularisation @sec-explicit-reg-nn]</span> involves **deliberately modifying the training objective or model**.

Examples:

- **Additive regularisation**  
  $$
  \mathcal{R}_n(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) + \lambda R(\boldsymbol{\theta})
  $$
  (e.g. $\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|^2$ penalty)

- **Dropout**  
  randomly sets some parameters or activations to zero during training

- **Architecture choices**  
  e.g. normalisation layers that restrict model behaviour

---

### Implicit Regularisation

<span class="xref-no-num">[Implicit regularisation @sec-implicit-reg-nn]</span> arises from the **training process itself**, without changing the objective.

Examples:

- **Optimisation effects**  
  stochastic optimisation tends to favour **wide minima**, which generalise better

- **Over-parameterisation**  
  surprisingly, very large models can generalise well due to optimisation dynamics

- **Early stopping**  
  stopping training before overfitting occurs

---

### Key Intuition

- **Explicit regularisation** = controlled, designed penalties  
- **Implicit regularisation** = emerges from how training is performed  

Both help prevent overfitting and improve generalisation.

---

### Key Points

- Explicit regularisation modifies the objective or model.
- Implicit regularisation comes from optimisation and training dynamics.
- Both are important in neural networks.
- Implicit regularisation is less well understood theoretically.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-nn-featurisation">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand how <span class="xref-no-num">[neural networks @sec-nn]</span> perform <span class="xref-no-num">[data-driven featurisation @sec-data-featurisation]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-nn-featurisation" hidden>

### Core Idea

Neural networks can be interpreted as performing **automatic (data-driven) featurisation**.

Instead of manually choosing features (as in <span class="xref-no-num">[variable selection @sec-variable-selection]</span> or <span class="xref-no-num">[dimensionality reduction @sec-dim-reduction]</span>), neural networks **learn features from the data**.

---

### Key Insight

An $L$-layer neural network can be written in the form

$$
f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})
=
\mathbf{W}^{(L)} \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})
+
\mathbf{b}^{(L)},
$$

where

$$
\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})
=
\sigma\big(
\mathbf{W}^{(L-1)} \sigma(\cdots \sigma(\mathbf{W}^{(1)} \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)}) \cdots)
\big).
$$

---

### Interpretation

- The function $\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})$ acts as a **feature map**.
- The final layer is just a **linear model** applied to these features.
- The features themselves depend on parameters learned from the data.

---

### Key Difference from Earlier Methods

- In earlier methods, features are:
  - **chosen manually**, or
  - **computed by a fixed rule** (e.g. PCA)

- In neural networks:
  - features are **learned automatically during training**

---

### Why This is Powerful

This allows neural networks to:

- learn **complex, nonlinear features**;
- adapt features specifically to the task;
- avoid manual feature engineering.

For example (conceptually):

- in image data, features may correspond to edges, shapes, or patterns;
- these would be difficult to design by hand.

---

### Interpretation Challenge

Although neural networks learn useful features:

- these features can be **difficult to interpret**;
- understanding learned features is an active research area.

---

### Key Points

- Neural networks perform **data-driven featurisation**.
- Hidden layers define a learned feature map $\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})$.
- The final layer is a linear model on these features.
- Features are learned from data, not specified in advance.
- This enables flexible and powerful models.

</div>
</div>

## Chapter 3 - Stochastic Optimisation

<span class="xref-no-num">[Chapter 3 @sec-stoch-opt]</span> studies how machine learning models are trained in practice by solving optimisation problems.

In previous chapters, only the training objectives such as <span class="xref-no-num">[empirical risk minimisation @sec-erm]</span> and <span class="xref-no-num">[regularised objectives @def-additive-reg]</span> were discussed. Chapter 3 focusses on the algorithms used to minimise these objectives.

The chapter introduces the main tools used in modern machine learning:

1. <span class="xref-no-num">[gradient descent @sec-grad-desc]</span>;
2. <span class="xref-no-num">[stochastic gradient descent @sec-sgd]</span> and its variants;
3. <span class="xref-no-num">[automatic differentiation @sec-autodiff]</span> (**not examinable**)

These methods enable efficient optimisation in high-dimensional settings and underpin the training of models such as <span class="xref-no-num">[neural networks @sec-nn]</span>.

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-stoch-opt-intro">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand why <span class="xref-no-num">[stochastic optimisation @sec-stoch-opt]</span> is used in machine learning.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-stoch-opt-intro" hidden>

### The Problem

Training a machine learning model typically involves solving an optimisation problem of the form

$$
\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \Theta}
\mathcal{R}_n(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}).
$$

In modern applications, this is challenging because:

- the parameter $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ is often **high-dimensional**;
- the dataset size $n$ can be **very large**;
- computing $\mathcal{R}_n$ requires summing over all data points;
- the objective may be **non-convex**, with many local minima.

---

### Why Stochastic Optimisation?

To address these issues, we use **stochastic optimisation**.

Key idea:

- replace the full dataset with **random subsets (mini-batches)**;
- approximate the objective or its gradient using these subsets.

---

### Advantages

This approach:

- is **computationally efficient** (avoids full dataset passes);
- scales to **large datasets**;
- allows **frequent parameter updates**;
- often finds solutions that **generalise well** in practice.

---

### Key Trade-off

- **Faster computation**  
  vs  
- **Noisy (approximate) optimisation**

Despite being approximate, stochastic methods are highly effective in practice.

---

### Key Points

- Exact optimisation is often too expensive in large-scale problems.
- Stochastic optimisation uses random subsets of data.
- It trades accuracy for speed and scalability.
- It is the standard approach in modern machine learning.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-gradient-descent">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand <span class="xref-no-num">[gradient descent @sec-grad-desc]</span>, including the update rule and the role of the learning rate.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-gradient-descent" hidden>

### Basic Idea

<span class="xref-no-num">[Gradient descent @sec-grad-desc]</span> is an iterative method for minimising an objective function such as the <span class="xref-no-num">[empirical risk @def-empirical-risk]</span>.

The idea is to:

- start from an initial parameter value $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$;
- repeatedly move in the direction of **steepest decrease** of the objective.

---

### Update Rule

The gradient descent update is

$$
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1}
=
\boldsymbol{\theta}_t
-
\epsilon
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{R}_n(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
\big|_{\boldsymbol{\theta} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_t}.
$$

- $\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{R}_n$ is the gradient of the objective;
- $\epsilon > 0$ is the **learning rate**.

---

### Role of the Learning Rate

The learning rate $\epsilon$ controls the step size:

- if $\epsilon$ is too **large**, updates may overshoot and fail to converge;
- if $\epsilon$ is too **small**, convergence is very slow.

Choosing $\epsilon$ appropriately is important in practice.

---

### Gradient of the Empirical Risk

Using the chain rule,

$$
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{R}_n(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
=
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{i=1}^n
\nabla_2 L(\mathbf{y}_i, f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_i))
\,
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_i).
$$

- $\nabla_2 L$ = derivative of the loss with respect to predictions;
- $\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ = sensitivity of the model output to parameters.

---

### Practical Considerations

- Gradient descent is typically run for a finite number of steps $T$.
- The final iterate $\boldsymbol{\theta}_T$ is taken as an approximation to the minimiser.
- Computing gradients is made practical by <span class="xref-no-num">[automatic differentiation @sec-autodiff]</span>.

---

### Key Points

- Gradient descent iteratively updates parameters using the gradient.
- The update moves in the direction of **steepest decrease**.
- The learning rate controls the step size.
- The gradient is computed using the chain rule.
- It is a fundamental method for training machine learning models.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-convex-functions">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand the definition and key properties of a <span class="xref-no-num">[convex function @def-convex-function]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-convex-functions" hidden>

### Definition

A differentiable function $F : \mathbb{R}^p \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is **convex** if

$$
F(\boldsymbol{\vartheta})
\geq
F(\boldsymbol{\theta})
+
\nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta})^\top (\boldsymbol{\vartheta} - \boldsymbol{\theta})
$$

for all $\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\vartheta} \in \mathbb{R}^p$.

---

### Intuition

- The function always lies **above its tangent line**.
- The graph has a **bowl-shaped** structure (no “dips”).

---

### Key Property

For convex functions:

$$
\nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_\star) = \mathbf{0}
\quad \Longrightarrow \quad
\boldsymbol{\theta}_\star \text{ is a global minimiser.}
$$

This is crucial:

- **local optimality = global optimality**

---

### Why This Matters

- Gradient-based methods (like <span class="xref-no-num">[gradient descent @sec-grad-desc]</span>) are much easier to analyse.
- No risk of getting stuck in “bad” local minima.

---

### Key Points

- Convexity ensures the function lies above its tangent.
- Any stationary point is a global minimum.
- This makes optimisation tractable and well-behaved.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-gd-convergence">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand the <span class="xref-no-num">[convergence of gradient descent @thm-gd]</span> for convex functions (statement and interpretation only).
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-gd-convergence" hidden>

### Result (Informal)

For a convex and differentiable function $F$, gradient descent produces a sequence $(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)$ such that

$$
\frac{1}{T}
\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}
F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)
-
F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_\star)
\;\; \text{is small for large } T,
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\theta}_\star$ is a minimiser of $F$.

---

### Interpretation

- The average value of $F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)$ gets close to the **optimal value**.
- Performance improves as:
  - number of iterations $T$ increases;
  - learning rate $\epsilon$ is chosen appropriately.

---

### Regret

The quantity

$$
\frac{1}{T}
\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}
F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)
-
F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_\star)
$$

is called the **regret**.

- measures how much worse we perform compared to the optimum;
- goes to **zero** as $T$ increases (with suitable $\epsilon$).

---

### Role of Learning Rate

- $\epsilon$ must be **small enough** for convergence;
- there is a trade-off:
  - too large → unstable updates;
  - too small → slow convergence.

---

### Key Takeaway

- For convex problems, gradient descent is **guaranteed to approach the global minimum**.
- This provides a theoretical justification for gradient-based methods.

---

### Key Points

- Gradient descent converges for convex objectives.
- The guarantee is in terms of **average performance (regret)**.
- Larger $T$ → better approximation.
- Learning rate choice is critical.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-sgd">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand <span class="xref-no-num">[stochastic gradient descent @sec-sgd]</span> and how it differs from <span class="xref-no-num">[gradient descent @sec-grad-desc]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-sgd" hidden>

### Motivation

In <span class="xref-no-num">[gradient descent @sec-grad-desc]</span>, each update requires computing

$$
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{R}_n(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
=
\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (\cdots),
$$

which involves **all $n$ data points**.

For large datasets, this is computationally expensive.

---

### Key Idea

<span class="xref-no-num">[Stochastic gradient descent @sec-sgd]</span> replaces the full gradient with an approximation using a **random subset (minibatch)**:

$$
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{R}_n(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
\approx
\frac{1}{m}
\sum_{j=1}^m
\nabla_2 L(\mathbf{y}_{i_j}, f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i_j}))
\,
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{i_j}).
$$

---

### Update Rule

$$
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1}
=
\boldsymbol{\theta}_t
-
\epsilon \, G_t(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t),
$$

where $G_t$ is a **stochastic gradient**.

---

### Key Properties

- $G_t$ is an **unbiased estimate** of the true gradient:
  $$
  \mathbb{E}[G_t(\boldsymbol{\theta})] = \nabla F(\boldsymbol{\theta})
  $$
- introduces **noise** into the updates
- cheaper per iteration than full gradient descent

---

### Trade-off

- Smaller minibatch size $m$:
  - faster computation
  - higher variance (noisier updates)

- Larger $m$:
  - more accurate gradient
  - higher computational cost

---

### Key Differences from Gradient Descent

| Gradient Descent | SGD |
|-----------------|-----|
| Uses all data | Uses minibatches |
| Accurate gradient | Noisy gradient |
| Expensive per step | Cheap per step |

---

### Key Points

- SGD approximates the gradient using random subsets of data.
- It is much more scalable than full gradient descent.
- Updates are noisy but efficient.
- It is the standard method used in practice.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-sgd-convergence">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand the <span class="xref-no-num">[convergence of stochastic gradient descent @thm-sgd]</span> (statement and interpretation only).
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-sgd-convergence" hidden>

### Result (Informal)

For a convex objective $F$, stochastic gradient descent produces iterates $(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)$ such that

$$
\frac{1}{T}
\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}
\mathbb{E}[F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)]
-
F(\boldsymbol{\theta}_\star)
$$

is small for large $T$.

---

### Interpretation

- On average, SGD gets close to the **optimal value**.
- Convergence is similar to <span class="xref-no-num">[gradient descent @thm-gd]</span>, but:
  - includes **expectation** due to randomness;
  - reflects **noisy updates**.

---

### Key Insight

- SGD behaves like gradient descent **on average**.
- Noise does not prevent convergence, but affects accuracy.

---

### Role of Learning Rate

- Same trade-off as gradient descent:
  - too large → unstable;
  - too small → slow.

---

### Key Takeaway

- SGD converges for convex problems under mild conditions.
- It provides a theoretical justification for using noisy gradients.

---

### Key Points

- SGD converges in expectation.
- Noise is introduced but controlled.
- Larger $T$ improves performance.
- Similar guarantees to gradient descent, but stochastic.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-autodiff">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic"> [{{< fa star >}}]{.advanced title="MAS8607 Content"} Understand <span class="xref-no-num">[automatic differentiation @sec-autodiff]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-autodiff" hidden>

### Core Idea

<span class="xref-no-num">[Automatic differentiation @sec-autodiff]</span> is a computational method for efficiently evaluating derivatives such as

$$
\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{R}_n(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}).
$$

It underpins modern machine learning frameworks (e.g. PyTorch, JAX).

---

### Why It Is Needed

Training methods such as:

- <span class="xref-no-num">[gradient descent @sec-grad-desc]</span>
- <span class="xref-no-num">[stochastic gradient descent @sec-sgd]</span>

require repeated computation of gradients.

For complex models (e.g. <span class="xref-no-num">[neural networks @sec-nn]</span>), computing these derivatives by hand is impractical.

---

### Key Property

Automatic differentiation computes derivatives:

- **exactly** (up to numerical precision);
- **efficiently**, even for very complex functions.

---

### Comparison with Numerical Differentiation

Finite-difference methods approximate derivatives:

$$
f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x+\delta) - f(x-\delta)}{2\delta}.
$$

However, these:

- are **approximate**;
- can be **numerically unstable**;
- are **computationally expensive** in high dimensions.

---

### Why Automatic Differentiation Is Better

- avoids approximation error;
- scales well to high-dimensional parameter spaces;
- enables efficient training of large models.

---

### Key Points

- Automatic differentiation computes gradients exactly and efficiently.
- It is essential for training modern machine learning models.
- It is superior to numerical differentiation in both accuracy and scalability.
- **This content is examinable for MAS8607 only.**

</div>
</div>

## Chapter 4 - Generalisation Error

<span class="xref-no-num">[Chapter 4 @sec-generalisation]</span> studies how well a trained <span class="xref-no-num">[machine learning model @def-ml-model]</span> performs on new data.

The central object of study is the **generalisation error**, which measures the gap between the performance of a trained model and the best possible model in the class (cf. <span class="xref-no-num">[risk @def-risk]</span>).

This chapter introduces:

1. the definition and intuition behind generalisation error;
2. [{{< fa star >}}]{.advanced title="MAS8607 Content"} basic generalisation error bounds for <span class="xref-no-num">[empirical risk minimisation @sec-erm]</span>;
3. [{{< fa star >}}]{.advanced title="MAS8607 Content"} related concepts such as sample complexity and the bias–variance trade-off;
4. the practical issue of <span class="xref-no-num">[domain shift @sec-domain-shift]</span>.

With the exception of the basic intuition, the mathematical analysis in this chapter is **examinable for MAS8607 students only**.

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-generalisation-error">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand the definition and intuition of the <span class="xref-no-num">[generalisation error @def-generalisation-error]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-generalisation-error" hidden>

### Definition

The <span class="xref-no-num">[generalisation error @def-generalisation-error]</span> is

$$
\mathcal{R}(f_n) - \min_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f),
$$

where:

- $\mathcal{R}(f)$ is the <span class="xref-no-num">[risk @def-risk]</span> (performance on the true data distribution);
- $f_n$ is the trained model (e.g. from <span class="xref-no-num">[empirical risk minimisation @sec-erm]</span>);
- $\mathcal{F}$ is the model class.

---

### Intuition

- $\mathcal{R}(f_n)$ = how well your trained model performs on **new data**;
- $\min_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f)$ = the **best possible performance** achievable within the model class.

So the generalisation error measures:

> how far your trained model is from the best possible model in $\mathcal{F}$.

---

### Why It Exists

Generalisation error arises because:

- we only observe a **finite dataset**;
- we optimise the <span class="xref-no-num">[empirical risk @def-empirical-risk]</span>, not the true risk;
- the empirical risk is only an **approximation** of the population risk.

---

### Key Properties

- Generalisation error is **always non-negative**;
- It depends on:
  - the **model class** $\mathcal{F}$;
  - the **amount of data** $n$;
  - the **training procedure**.

---

### Key Interpretation

- Small generalisation error ⇒ model is close to optimal.
- Large generalisation error ⇒ model is suboptimal (e.g. due to overfitting or poor model choice).

---

### Key Points

- Generalisation error measures the gap to the best possible model.
- It arises from finite data and approximate optimisation.
- It is the central quantity in evaluating machine learning models.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-hoeffding">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
[{{< fa star >}}]{.advanced title="MAS8607 Content"} Understand <span class="xref-no-num">[Hoeffding's inequality @prp-hoeffding]</span>. **Note: you are not expected to be remember this result for the exam or its proof**.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-hoeffding" hidden>

### Statement

Let $Z_1, \dots, Z_n$ be independent random variables with mean $\mu$ and values in $[0,1]$. Then for any $t > 0$,

$$
\mathbb{P}\left(
\left|
\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i - \mu
\right|
\geq t
\right)
\leq
2 \exp(-2 n t^2).
$$

---

### Intuition

- The sample average
  $$
  \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i
  $$
  concentrates around the true mean $\mu$.

- Large deviations from $\mu$ become **exponentially unlikely** as $n$ increases.

---

### Why It Matters

- Gives a **high-probability bound** on estimation error.
- Key tool for analysing:
  - <span class="xref-no-num">[empirical risk @def-empirical-risk]</span> vs  
  - <span class="xref-no-num">[population risk @def-risk]</span>.

---

### Key Behaviour

- Larger $n$ ⇒ tighter concentration.
- Larger deviation $t$ ⇒ exponentially smaller probability.

---

### Key Points

- Hoeffding’s inequality bounds how far averages deviate from expectations.
- Probability of large deviations decays exponentially in $n$.
- It is a core tool in generalisation analysis.
- **This content is examinable for MAS8607 only.**

</div>
</div>


<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-gen-bound">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
[{{< fa star >}}]{.advanced title="MAS8607 Content"} Understand the <span class="xref-no-num">[generalisation error bound @thm-generalisation-error]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-gen-bound" hidden>

### Statement

For a finite model class $\mathcal{F}$ and loss $L \in [0,1]$, with probability at least $1 - \delta$,

$$
\mathcal{R}(f_n) - \min_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f)
\leq
\sqrt{
\frac{2}{n}
\log \frac{2|\mathcal{F}|}{\delta}
}.
$$

---

### Interpretation

This bounds the <span class="xref-no-num">[generalisation error @def-generalisation-error]</span>.

It shows that:

- the trained model is close to the best possible model in $\mathcal{F}$;
- the gap shrinks as the dataset size $n$ increases.

---

### Key Dependencies

The bound depends on:

- **Sample size $n$**  
  → larger $n$ ⇒ smaller error

- **Model size $|\mathcal{F}|$**  
  → larger model class ⇒ larger error

- **Confidence level $\delta$**  
  → higher confidence (smaller $\delta$) ⇒ looser bound

---

### Intuition

There is a trade-off:

- More flexible models (large $\mathcal{F}$):
  - lower bias
  - higher variance

- Simpler models (small $\mathcal{F}$):
  - higher bias
  - lower variance

This is the **bias–variance trade-off**.

---

### Key Takeaway

- With enough data, empirical risk minimisation performs well.
- But performance depends on balancing:
  - model complexity;
  - dataset size.

---

### Key Points

- Generalisation error decreases as $n$ increases.
- Larger model classes increase uncertainty.
- Confidence level affects the tightness of the bound.
- Captures the bias–variance trade-off.
- **This content is examinable for MAS8607 only.**

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-gen-proof">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
[{{< fa star >}}]{.advanced title="MAS8607 Content"} Understand the key steps in the <span class="xref-no-num">[proof @prf-generalisation-error]</span> of the <span class="xref-no-num">[generalisation error bound @thm-generalisation-error]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-gen-proof" hidden>

### What You Are Expected to Know

You are **not** expected to reproduce the full proof, but you should understand:

- the **main tools used**;
- the **logical structure of the argument**;
- how the final bound is obtained.

---

### Step 1 — Apply Hoeffding (pointwise control)

For each fixed model $f \in \mathcal{F}$:

$$
\mathbb{P}\left(
|\mathcal{R}_n(f) - \mathcal{R}(f)| \geq t
\right)
\leq
2 \exp(-2nt^2).
$$

Interpretation: empirical risk is close to population risk **for a fixed model**.

---

### Step 2 — Union bound (uniform control)

We want this to hold **for all $f \in \mathcal{F}$ simultaneously**.

Use the union bound:

$$
\mathbb{P}\left(
\exists f \in \mathcal{F} \text{ such that } |\mathcal{R}_n(f) - \mathcal{R}(f)| \geq t
\right)
\leq
2|\mathcal{F}| e^{-2nt^2}.
$$

Key idea: control worst-case deviation over the whole model class.

---

### Step 3 — Uniform convergence

With high probability:

$$
|\mathcal{R}_n(f) - \mathcal{R}(f)| < t
\quad \text{for all } f \in \mathcal{F}.
$$

This is called **uniform convergence**.

---

### Step 4 — Relate ERM to optimal model

Let:

- $f_n$ = empirical risk minimiser  
- $f_\star$ = true (population) risk minimiser  

Then:

$$
\mathcal{R}(f_n)
\leq
\mathcal{R}_n(f_n) + t
\leq
\mathcal{R}_n(f_\star) + t
\leq
\mathcal{R}(f_\star) + 2t.
$$

Key logic:

1. empirical ≈ population (uniform convergence)
2. ERM minimises empirical risk
3. combine inequalities

---

### Step 5 — Solve for $t$

Set probability level:

$$
\delta = 2|\mathcal{F}| e^{-2nt^2}
$$
Rearranging gives:
$$
t =
\sqrt{
\frac{1}{2n}
\log\left(\frac{2|\mathcal{F}|}{\delta}\right)
}.
$$

Substitute into bound.

---

### Final Result

$$
\mathcal{R}(f_n) - \mathcal{R}(f_\star)
\leq
\sqrt{
\frac{2}{n}
\log \frac{2|\mathcal{F}|}{\delta}
}.
$$

---

### Big Picture

The proof combines:

- **concentration inequality** (Hoeffding)
- **union bound**
- **ERM optimality**

to show:

> empirical risk minimisation works because empirical risk approximates population risk **uniformly**.

---

### Key Points

- Hoeffding ⇒ control for a fixed model.
- Union bound ⇒ extend to all models.
- Uniform convergence ⇒ key concept.
- ERM + uniform convergence ⇒ generalisation bound.
- You should understand the **flow of the argument**, not memorise every line.
- **This content is examinable for MAS8607 only.**

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-domain-shift-content">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand the concept of <span class="xref-no-num">[domain shift @sec-domain-shift]</span> and its implications for machine learning performance.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-domain-shift-content" hidden>

### Core Idea

In theoretical formulations of supervised learning, we assume that:

- training data are sampled from a distribution $P$;
- future (deployment) data are drawn from the same distribution.

In practice, this assumption is often violated.

---

### Definition

**Domain shift** refers to the situation where the data distribution at deployment differs from that observed during training.

Equivalently, the deployment risk $\mathcal{R}_\star$ differs from the training risk $\mathcal{R}$.

---

### Why It Occurs

Common sources of domain shift include:

- **Temporal effects**  
  Data evolve over time (e.g. footfall, financial data).

- **Population differences**  
  Training and deployment populations differ (e.g. medical datasets).

- **Sampling bias**  
  Training data are not representative of the true environment.

---

### Why It Matters

Even if:

- empirical risk is small, and  
- generalisation error is small,

the model may still perform poorly if the deployment distribution differs from the training distribution.

---

### Extended Risk Decomposition

The deployment risk can be decomposed as:

$$
\mathcal{R}_\star(f_n)
\leq
\underbrace{
\max_{f \in \mathcal{F}} |\mathcal{R}_\star(f) - \mathcal{R}(f)|
}_{\text{domain shift}}
+
\underbrace{
\min_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(f)
}_{\text{bias}}
+
\underbrace{
\sqrt{\frac{2}{n} \log \frac{2|\mathcal{F}|}{\delta}}
}_{\text{variance}}
$$

You **do not need to memorise this formula**, but you should understand the key terms and their implications.

---

### Interpretation

- **Bias** reflects limitations of the model class $\mathcal{F}$.
- **Variance** reflects uncertainty due to finite data.
- **Domain shift** reflects mismatch between training and deployment environments.

Domain shift is not controlled by standard generalisation bounds.

---

### Key Insight

Generalisation theory assumes that training and test data are drawn from the same distribution.  
It does not account for domain shift.

---

### Practical Implications

- Models should be validated on data that reflect deployment conditions.
- Distributional assumptions must be carefully assessed.
- Domain shift is a major cause of:
  - degraded performance,
  - unreliable predictions,
  - ethical concerns (e.g. fairness across populations).

---

### Key Points

- Domain shift is a mismatch between training and deployment data distributions.
- It is distinct from generalisation error.
- Standard machine learning theory does not address it.
- It is often the dominant factor in real-world model performance.

</div>
</div>

## Chapter 5 - Online Supervised Learning

<span class="xref-no-num">[Chapter 5 @sec-online-supervised-learning]</span> studies a different paradigm for training machine learning models, where data arrive sequentially over time rather than being available in a fixed dataset.

Unlike the standard (offline) setting, where a model is trained once and then deployed, online learning continuously updates the model as new observations are received.

This chapter introduces:

1. the formal definition of an <span class="xref-no-num">[online supervised learning task @def-online-ml-task]</span>;
2. the distinction between environments with and without feedback;
3. the concept of cumulative loss as a performance measure over time.

The **examinable content** from this chapter is **entirely intuitive and conceptual**, rather than mathematical.

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-offline-vs-online-content">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand the difference between <strong>offline</strong> and <strong>online</strong> supervised learning.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-offline-vs-online-content" hidden>

### Offline (Batch) Learning

In the standard supervised learning setting:

- we are given a **fixed dataset**  
  $$
  \{(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{y}_i)\}_{i=1}^n;
  $$
- the model is trained **once** by minimising empirical risk;
- after training, the model is **deployed without further updates**.

**Key feature:**  
All data are available in advance.

---

### Online Learning

In online supervised learning:

- data arrive **sequentially over time**;
- at time $t$, the model is trained using data  
  $$
  \{(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{y}_i)\}_{i=1}^{t-1};
  $$
- the model is **updated continuously** as new data arrive.

**Key feature:**  
The model must adapt in real time.

---

### Key Differences

| Aspect | Offline Learning | Online Learning |
|------|----------------|----------------|
| Data availability | Fixed dataset | Sequential / streaming |
| Training | One-off | Continuous updates |
| Objective | Minimise empirical risk | Minimise cumulative loss |
| Adaptation | None after training | Adapts over time |
| Typical use | Static datasets | Dynamic environments |

---

### When Online Learning Is Needed

Online learning is particularly useful when:

- data arrive in a **stream**;
- storing all past data is impractical;
- the underlying distribution may **change over time**  
  (cf. <span class="xref-no-num">[domain shift @sec-domain-shift]</span>).

---

### Key Points

- Offline learning assumes a fixed dataset and static environment.
- Online learning updates the model sequentially.
- The performance measure changes from **risk** to **cumulative loss**.
- Online learning is essential in **dynamic or real-time settings**.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-bandits-content">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand the <span class="xref-no-num">[multi-armed bandit problem @sec-bandits]</span> and the concept of <strong>regret</strong>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-bandits-content" hidden>

### Core Idea

A **multi-armed bandit** models sequential decision-making under uncertainty:

- there are $B$ possible actions (bandits / arms);
- each action $i$ has an unknown expected reward $\mu_i$;
- at each time $t$, we choose an action and observe a reward.

---

### The Challenge

We do **not know** the values of $\mu_i$ in advance.

To perform well, we must:

- **explore**: try different actions to learn their rewards;
- **exploit**: choose the best-known action to maximise reward.

This creates the fundamental **exploration–exploitation trade-off**.

---

### Objective

Let

$$
\mu_\star = \max_{1 \leq i \leq B} \mu_i
$$

be the best possible expected reward.

The goal is to minimise the **regret**:

$$
\mu_\star - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T R_t
$$

---

### Interpretation of Regret

- Measures how much reward we **lose** compared to always choosing the best arm.
- If we always pick the optimal bandit, regret is $0$.
- In practice, regret is positive because we must explore.

---

### Why Regret Arises

- The optimal action is **unknown initially**.
- Learning requires **trying suboptimal actions**.
- This incurs a temporary loss in reward.

---

### Examples of Bandit Problems

- **Online advertising**  
  Selecting adverts to maximise click-through rates.

- **Clinical trials**  
  Allocating treatments while learning effectiveness.

---

### Key Insight

Bandits are a simple instance of online learning where:

- decisions are made sequentially;
- feedback is limited (we only observe the reward of the chosen action);
- performance is measured over time via **regret**.

---

### Key Points

- Multi-armed bandit = sequential decision problem with unknown rewards.
- Must balance **exploration** and **exploitation**.
- Performance is measured using **regret**, not risk.
- Regret quantifies the cost of learning.

</div>
</div>



## Chapter 6 - Beyond Supervised Learning

## Chapter 7 - Ethics of Machine Learning

<span class="xref-no-num">[Chapter 7 @sec-ethics]</span> considers the ethical issues that arise when machine learning models are deployed in real-world settings.

While earlier chapters focused on the mathematical and statistical foundations of machine learning, this chapter highlights that technical performance alone is not sufficient; the use of machine learning systems can have significant societal consequences.

The chapter discusses a range of ethical considerations, including:

1. bias and fairness in model predictions;
2. responsibility and accountability for decisions made by models;
3. privacy and consent in the use of data;
4. broader societal impacts, such as environmental cost and labour market effects.

An important learning outcome is to be able to identify and explain ethical issues that may arise in a given machine learning application.

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-bias-fairness">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand issues of <span class="xref-no-num">[bias and fairness @iss-bias-and-fairness]</span> in machine learning.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-bias-fairness" hidden>

### What is the Issue?

Machine learning models are trained on data. If the training data are:

- **unrepresentative**, or  
- reflect existing **societal biases**,  

then the trained model may produce **biased or unfair predictions**.

---

### Examples

- A medical model trained only on one population (e.g. a single genetic background) may perform poorly on others.
- A financial model may assign different outcomes (e.g. loan rates) to similar individuals based on features correlated with protected characteristics.

---

### Key Idea

Bias can arise because the model:

- learns patterns present in the data;
- cannot distinguish between **correlation** and **fairness**.

---

### Defining Fairness

A central difficulty is that **fairness is not uniquely defined**.

Different notions include:

- equal outcomes across groups;
- equal error rates across groups;
- decisions based only on “relevant” features.

These definitions can conflict with each other.

---

### Trade-off with Performance

Improving fairness may:

- require constraining the model;
- reduce performance with respect to the original objective (e.g. prediction accuracy or <span class="xref-no-num">[risk @def-risk]</span>).

---

### Mitigation

Fairness can be incorporated by modifying the training objective, for example:

$$
\mathcal{R}_n(f) + \lambda R(f),
$$

where $R(f)$ penalises unfair behaviour.

(See <span class="xref-no-num">[regularisation @sec-linear-regularisation]</span>.)

---

### Key Points

- Bias arises from data and modelling choices.
- Fairness is difficult to define and measure.
- Different definitions of fairness may conflict.
- There is often a trade-off between fairness and performance.
- Regularisation can be used to encourage fair behaviour.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-autonomy-responsibility">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand issues of **autonomy and responsibility** in machine learning (@iss-autonomy).
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-autonomy-responsibility" hidden>

### What is the Issue?

When a machine learning model is deployed in the real world, it may make decisions that have **serious consequences** (e.g. financial, legal, or physical harm).

This raises the question:

- **Who is responsible** when something goes wrong?

---

### Sources of Failure

Harmful outcomes may arise from:

- errors in code (bugs);
- poor or biased training data;
- incorrect modelling assumptions;
- **adversarial attacks** (e.g. data poisoning).

Responsibility may depend on the source of the failure.

---

### Accountability

Possible parties include:

- the model developer;
- the organisation deploying the model;
- regulators or oversight bodies.

In practice, responsibility is often **unclear and shared**.

---

### Autonomy vs Human Oversight

Machine learning systems can operate with a high degree of **autonomy**.

Key questions:

- Should humans remain **in the loop** for important decisions?
- Should fully automated decision-making be allowed in high-stakes settings?

---

### Transparency and Explainability

There is increasing demand for:

- the ability to **challenge decisions** made by models;
- **explanations** of how decisions were made.

However:

- many models (e.g. neural networks) are difficult to interpret;
- models may be protected as **corporate intellectual property**.

---

### Regulation and Control

Questions arise about:

- whether AI systems should be **regulated**;
- whether outputs (e.g. political content) should be controlled;
- how to balance innovation with **safety and accountability**.

---

### Key Points

- Machine learning systems can cause real-world harm.
- Responsibility for decisions is often unclear.
- Failures can arise from data, models, or external attacks.
- There is a tension between autonomy and human oversight.
- Transparency and regulation are central ethical challenges.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-ai-warfare">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand issues of <span class="xref-no-num">[AI in warfare @iss-warfare]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-ai-warfare" hidden>

### What is the Issue?

Machine learning and AI are increasingly being used in **military contexts**, including:

- surveillance;
- target identification;
- autonomous or semi-autonomous weapons systems.

This raises serious **ethical and legal concerns**.

---

### Legal Considerations

Military use of AI must comply with international law, including:

- the **Geneva Convention**;
- rules prohibiting attacks on civilians.

Key question:

- how can we ensure that decisions made by a model are **legally compliant**?

---

### Human Oversight

A central issue is whether **life-and-death decisions** should be:

- fully automated; or  
- subject to **human control (“human-in-the-loop”)**.

---

### Risk and Failure

Machine learning systems can:

- fail unpredictably;
- behave incorrectly in unfamiliar situations;
- be vulnerable to adversarial manipulation.

In a military setting, such failures could have **catastrophic consequences**.

---

### Responsibility

As with <span class="xref-no-num">[autonomy and responsibility @iss-autonomy]</span>:

- it may be unclear who is accountable for decisions made by AI systems in warfare.

---

### Broader Ethical Questions

- Should AI be used in warfare at all?
- Does increased effectiveness justify ethical risks?
- What level of regulation or international agreement is needed?

---

### Key Points

- AI is increasingly used in military decision-making.
- There are serious concerns about legality and civilian safety.
- Human oversight is a key ethical issue.
- Failures can have catastrophic consequences.
- Responsibility and regulation remain open questions.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-consent-data">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand issues of <span class="xref-no-num">[consent to data use @iss-consent]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-consent-data" hidden>

### What is the Issue?

Machine learning models require **large amounts of data**, often collected from:

- the internet (e.g. text, images);
- personal or institutional records (e.g. health data).

This raises questions about **consent and ownership** of data.

---

### Copyright and Data Use

- Training data may include **copyrighted material**.
- Data are often collected without explicit permission from creators.

Key questions:

- Should creators receive **compensation** for use of their data?
- Is training a model fundamentally different from copying content?

---

### Personal Data and Consent

Even when data are **anonymised**, concerns remain:

- individuals may not be aware their data are used;
- anonymisation may not fully prevent **re-identification**.

Example:

- health records used for research or commercial purposes.

---

### Trade-offs

There is a tension between:

- **innovation and progress** in AI;
- **individual rights** to privacy and consent.

Relaxing restrictions may:

- accelerate research and development;

but may also:

- reduce protections for individuals.

---

### Regulation

The legal framework is currently:

- evolving;
- often unclear.

Governments are actively considering how to regulate:

- data usage;
- copyright in machine learning.

---

### Key Points

- Machine learning relies on large-scale data collection.
- Consent is often unclear or absent.
- Copyright and ownership of training data are contested.
- Anonymisation does not guarantee privacy.
- There is a trade-off between innovation and individual protection.
- Regulation in this area is still developing.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-environmental-impact">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand issues of <span class="xref-no-num">[environmental impact @iss-environmental-impact]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-environmental-impact" hidden>

### What is the Issue?

Training large machine learning models can require **substantial computational resources**, leading to:

- high electricity usage;
- significant carbon emissions;
- additional resource costs (e.g. cooling, water).

---

### Scale of the Problem

Modern models (e.g. large language models) can require:

- **massive datasets**;
- **large-scale parallel computation** (e.g. GPUs running for weeks).

This leads to **very high energy consumption**.

---

### Trade-offs

There is a tension between:

- **environmental cost**, and  
- **societal benefit** (e.g. improved technology, productivity).

Key questions:

- Are these energy costs justified?
- Should there be limits on large-scale model training?

---

### Broader Impacts

- Growth in data centres increases overall energy demand.
- Environmental impact may increase if many organisations compete to train large models.

---

### Regulation and Policy

Possible responses include:

- improving energy efficiency;
- using renewable energy sources;
- regulating large-scale compute usage.

---

### Key Points

- Machine learning can have a significant environmental footprint.
- Training large models requires substantial energy.
- There is a trade-off between innovation and sustainability.
- The cumulative impact of widespread model training is a concern.
- Policy and regulation may play an important role.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-job-impact">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand issues of <span class="xref-no-num">[job displacement and labour market impact @iss-job-impact]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-job-impact" hidden>

### What is the Issue?

Machine learning and AI have the potential to **transform the labour market**, including:

- automating existing jobs;
- creating new types of work;
- changing required skill sets.

---

### Job Displacement

Some roles may be at risk, particularly:

- repetitive or routine tasks;
- roles in manufacturing, logistics, and customer service.

---

### Uncertainty

The overall impact is difficult to predict:

- past technological advances have both **destroyed and created jobs**;
- new capabilities (e.g. generative models) can disrupt unexpected sectors.

---

### Job Creation

AI may also create:

- roles in development, maintenance, and deployment;
- new industries and services.

---

### Transition Challenges

Key concerns include:

- speed of change;
- ability of workers to **retrain or adapt**;
- potential short-term increases in unemployment or inequality.

---

### Key Questions

- Which sectors will be most affected?
- Will the overall impact be positive or negative?
- How will this affect future career paths?

---

### Key Points

- AI can both displace and create jobs.
- The net effect is uncertain and context-dependent.
- Rapid change may create social and economic challenges.
- Adaptation and reskilling are important considerations.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-inequality">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand issues of <span class="xref-no-num">[inequality @iss-inequality]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-inequality" hidden>

### What is the Issue?

Machine learning and AI may **affect different groups unequally**, potentially:

- benefiting some individuals or regions more than others;
- widening existing social or economic inequalities.

---

### Potential Risks

- Wealthy organisations and nations may have greater access to:
  - data;
  - computational resources;
  - expertise.

- This may lead to **concentration of power and wealth**.

---

### Democratising Potential

On the other hand, AI tools (e.g. chatbots) may:

- provide widespread access to knowledge;
- lower barriers to education and productivity.

This could have a **democratising effect**.

---

### Key Tension

- **Inequality may increase** due to uneven access to resources;  
vs  
- **Inequality may decrease** due to wider access to powerful tools.

---

### Key Points

- AI may either exacerbate or reduce inequality.
- Outcomes depend on access to technology and resources.
- Distribution of benefits is a central concern.
- The long-term impact is uncertain.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-human-interaction">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand issues of <span class="xref-no-num">[human interaction @iss-human-interaction]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-human-interaction" hidden>

### What is the Issue?

AI is increasingly integrated into everyday life, influencing how people:

- interact with technology;
- communicate with each other;
- form relationships.

---

### Societal Impact

AI systems (e.g. virtual assistants, chatbots) may:

- change patterns of communication;
- reduce or replace certain forms of human interaction;
- influence behaviour and decision-making.

---

### Human–AI Relationships

There is evidence that people may:

- form emotional or personal connections with AI systems;
- rely on AI for companionship or advice.

This raises concerns about:

- dependency;
- manipulation;
- psychological effects.

---

### Vulnerable Groups

Concerns may be greater for:

- children;
- individuals more susceptible to influence.

This raises questions about **appropriate safeguards and regulation**.

---

### Key Questions

- How should AI systems interact with users?
- Should there be limits on AI influence?
- Should children’s interaction with AI be regulated?

---

### Key Points

- AI is changing human interaction patterns.
- Human–AI relationships raise new ethical concerns.
- Vulnerable users may require additional protections.
- The societal impact is still evolving.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-trust-veracity">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand issues of <span class="xref-no-num">[veracity and trust @iss-trust]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-trust-veracity" hidden>

### What is the Issue?

Advances in AI (e.g. text-to-image, text-to-video) make it possible to generate highly realistic synthetic content.

This creates challenges for **trust and authenticity**.

---

### Risks

- AI-generated content may be:
  - misleading;
  - difficult to distinguish from real data;
  - used for misinformation or manipulation.

- This can undermine trust in:
  - media;
  - institutions;
  - digital information.

---

### Lack of Safeguards

Currently:

- there is no universal system for verifying authenticity;
- regulation is limited or evolving.

---

### Key Questions

- How can we detect AI-generated content?
- Should content be labelled or regulated?
- What responsibilities do creators and platforms have?

---

### Broader Impact

- Reduced trust in information may affect:
  - education;
  - politics;
  - public discourse.

---

### Key Points

- AI enables realistic synthetic content generation.
- This creates challenges for trust and authenticity.
- Misinformation risks are significant.
- Regulation and detection methods are still developing.

</div>
</div>

      header.setAttribute('aria-expanded', !expanded);
